title: What flexible means on a fixed project
metaTitle: What flexible means when scope is fixed
excerpt: Flexible on a fixed project means you can swap a section when you learn something. It does not mean the edge of the work moves every week. Say which agreement you bought.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug. The desk has an edge, the way a fixed project should.
caption: A desk with a clear edge around the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What can change inside a fixed website project?
faqs.answer: You can replace or remove a section when it is failing the goal you already agreed, using the type, color, and templates you accepted. You can cut scope and keep the date. You can reorder a page so the price or the offer shows up sooner. Write the swap in a sentence so the build does not implement last week's memory.

faqs.question: What counts as a new project instead?
faqs.answer: A new template, a new audience on the same page, a shop, a login, a payment flow, or a new visual system after the system was approved. Each one moves the edge. Say so, then defer it, decline it, or quote it and move the date. Do not absorb it as a tweak.

faqs.question: How do you stay flexible without losing the launch?
faqs.answer: Keep a weekly list with the request, whether it is inside the edge, and what it does to the date. Ideas that do not fit go to a parking lot for after launch. One approver decides. Five people each swapping a section will turn the site into a hallway and spend the week you needed to build.

markdown:
A fixed scope website project can still be flexible, if you say which kind of flexible you bought. Flexible means you can swap a section when you learn something true about the audience or the offer. It does not mean the edge of the project moves every week. Those are different agreements. Buying one and expecting the other is how a calm project turns into a negotiation.

Write the edge down. Then write the kind of swap that stays inside it. Everything else is a change, with a date and a cost you accept on purpose.

## What stays still

The edge is the list you already priced. The templates. The states you included. The form, the CMS, the integrations. The number of feedback rounds. The languages. Whether a shop or a product login is in or out. That list is the project. Flexibility does not erase it. It tells you how to spend attention inside it.

The goal stays still too. “A stranger can tell what this company does and how to talk to you.” If a swap serves that goal, it is in the spirit of the work. If a swap adds a second audience, a second product, or a second brand, it is a different goal. Name it as a different goal before anyone moves a frame.

Dates stay still unless you move them out loud. A flexible section does not come with a flexible launch. If the launch is fixed, the swaps have to fit the days left. A swap that eats the week you needed for build is not free. It spends the launch. Say that when you accept it.

The people who may change the edge stay still. One approver. Feedback from others can inform them. It does not arrive as a parallel project. Five stakeholders each “just swapping a section” will swap the site into a hallway. The approver picks.

Hanabi’s work is design and production code: Figma for the decisions, Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind for the site. A swap inside that system is a component change. A swap that throws out the system is a new engagement. The difference should be obvious in the notes, not discovered in the invoice tone.

## What a swap inside the edge looks like

A swap replaces a section that is failing the goal with a section that might serve it better, using the type, color, and components you already accepted. The hero talks about the wrong product, so you rewrite the hero around the right one. The proof is a logo wall that means nothing, so you replace it with one concrete story you already have permission to tell. The form asks for eight fields, so you cut it to four. These are the same page, aimed better.

A swap can change order. Move the price up. Move the manifesto down. Cut a section that repeats the previous one. Reordering inside the agreed templates is the ordinary work of design. It should not require a change order. It should require a decision, recorded, so the build does not implement last week’s order.

A swap can drop scope. Doing less is always inside a fixed project. If you learn you do not need the blog at launch, take it off the list and keep the date. Do not fill the hole with a different feature of similar size and call it even, unless the estimate’s owner agrees the sizes match. “Even” is often how a shop appears in a marketing-site contract.

Write the swap in a sentence. “Replace the partner logos with one paragraph on Thomas Bewick’s editorial site, linking to the piece, because logos were not proof.” The sentence keeps the change reviewable. A vibe in a meeting will be remembered three different ways by Thursday.

## What moves the edge

These are new work, even if each one sounds small in the moment.

A new template. A careers page, a second product line, a journal with its own layout. If it was not on the list, it is not a swap. It is a template you did not design rules for.

A new audience on the same page. “Also make it speak to investors and to recruits” on a page built for buyers. That is a new goal. It usually ruins the first one. Park it or reprice it.

A shop, a login, or a payment flow added after kickoff. These bring states, accounts, and support. They are not a section. Down the Cove’s public scope is an ecommerce migration and redesign. That scope is chosen at the start. It is not a flexible extra on a brochure site.

A new integration with a vendor you have not opened. Booking tools, CRMs, custom data. Each one has a failure mode. Budget a spike or a line. Do not hide it inside “we’ll just connect it.”

A visual system change after the system was approved. New type, a new palette, a different logo treatment across every template. That is a rebrand passing as a tweak. It touches every screen you already called done.

Unlimited rounds of a new direction. The first direction was the project. A second direction is a second project that happens to reuse the domain name. You may buy it. Call it that, and move the date.

## How to say yes without losing the date

Keep a change list with three columns: the request, whether it is inside the edge, and what it does to the date. Review it once a week with the approver. Anything inside the edge is scheduled into the remaining days or it waits until after launch. Anything outside the edge is declined, deferred, or priced.

Defer is a real answer. A parking lot for good ideas protects the launch. The parking lot is not a promise to do the ideas for free in the launch week. It is a list you can read when the site is up and you know more.

When a request is outside, say the sentence plainly. “That is a new template. We can add it after launch, or we can move launch and quote it.” Then stop talking until they choose. Filling the silence with a compromise you cannot build is how the edge dissolves.

If you are the founder, resist the weekly idea unless it changes the goal. Write it down yourself and look at it on Friday. Many of them will look smaller once the current page is further along. The ones that remain can be the next engagement.

Staff the decision. A studio cannot be flexible if every swap waits four days for a founder who is traveling and then arrives as five swaps at once. The fixed project assumes a person who can say yes or no inside the week. Put that person in the agreement as clearly as you put the template list.

## Flexible craft, fixed promise

Inside the edge, the craft should stay flexible. Copy can tighten. A section can disappear. A component can be reused instead of redrawn. That is how quality goes up without a new invoice. A team that freezes every pixel at kickoff will ship the kickoff’s mistakes. A team that freezes nothing will ship nothing.

The promise to the outside world is the fixed part. What the site is for, when it will be up, and what “up” includes. Internal flexibility serves that promise. It does not replace it. If you learn the promise was wrong, stop and rewrite the promise. Do not trickle a new company out through weekly swaps and hope the date still means something.

Document the final edge at launch. Templates that shipped, templates that were cut, ideas parked. The next person who wants a “small addition” can see what the project was. The client portal, when you use one, is a reasonable home for that note and for the brand files. The repository is the home for the code those files became.

Google’s notes on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) are about public pages, and they still describe the discipline. Make the thing for a person, and keep it reliable. A fixed project that stays aimed at one reader will do that. A project that changes reader every Friday will publish a page nobody can quote.

## A sentence you can put in the agreement

Use language you would say on a call. “We can replace or remove sections inside the agreed templates when we learn something, within the rounds and the date. A new template, a shop, a product login, or a new audience is a change we will quote.” That is flexible and fixed at the same time. It is specific enough to prevent a fight, and short enough to remember.

Read it at kickoff. Read it again the first time someone brings a beloved new page. The second reading is the one that matters. Agreements that are only read at signing are decorations.

If the sentence does not match what you thought you bought, fix the sentence before the work starts. A mismatch in week one is a conversation. A mismatch in week six is a dispute about money and taste at once, which is the worst time to discover the definition.

Once the edge is clear, the weeks only work if you also agree how you will talk. [Communication during a four-week build](/blog/communication-during-a-four-week-build) is the next piece. It covers who answers, and what a same-day response covers, so flexibility does not turn into silence.
